sections.h2: What does the Summit County Recorder Division do?
sections.html:
It records and preserves documents that touch real estate in Summit County. The Recorder Division sits inside the Fiscal Office, so the same elected Fiscal Officer who bills property tax also oversees recording. Deeds, mortgages and liens make up the core, and the division also keeps partnership papers, zoning amendments, military discharges, living wills and medical powers of attorney.

Every record except military discharges is open to the public. Online search covers documents from 1988 forward, and an Index Book Archive Viewer reaches records from 1840 to 1988. The division states that it does not run title or property searches, so a buyer's title company handles that part. The posted turnaround is 3 to 5 working days.

The Fiscal Office moved its divisions to temporary quarters during renovation of the Ohio Building at 175 S. Main St. in Akron. Call the division, or write recorder@summitoh.net, before delivering paper to a counter.

sections.h2: What steps take a Summit County deed from signature to recorded?
sections.html:
A deed passes through the Fiscal Office's transfer desk first and the recording desk second. The sequence below follows the Fiscal Office's property transfer page and its recording guide.

  1. Sign the deed and have the signature acknowledged before an official such as a notary, as R.C. 5301.01 requires.
  2. Bring the deed and the conveyance fee statement, DTE Form 100, or the exemption statement, DTE Form 100 (EX), to the Property Transfer Department. It approves the legal description and the conveyance.
  3. Meet the 3:30 p.m. cutoff if you want the title transfer finished that business day.
  4. Present the approved deed to the Recorder Division with recording fees on a separate check.

The guide asks for legible documents, typed names beneath every signature, a full legal description on first recordings, references to earlier recorded documents, a return address and phone number, numbered exhibits, and a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Several e-recording vendors work with the office: Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners Network. A title company in a cash sale usually files this way.

sections.h2: What does recording a deed cost in Summit County?
sections.html:
Summit County recording and transfer fees as posted on the Fiscal Office fee page
ChargePosted amount
Basic recording$34.00 for two pages, $8.00 for each added page
Non-compliant document$20.00 per document
Cross reference$4.00 each
Conveyance fee$4.00 per $1,000 of sale price, rounded up to the next $100
Lot fee50 cents per lot in the legal description, exempt or not
Certification$1.00 per document

Fees come from R.C. 317.32. For two pages of a standard deed, the statute sets a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee, then $4 plus $4 for each page after, and it lets a county add a document preservation surcharge of up to $5. The Summit page shows $34 and $8 with no surcharge line. Ask the Recording Division to confirm the total before you write the check.

Copies by mail run $4, plus $1 for certification, with a self-addressed stamped envelope, according to the division's FAQ. The functions page separately lists $2 per page for copies. Military discharges are recorded at no charge.

sections.h2: Who pays the conveyance fee, and is there a transfer tax?
sections.html:
The seller does. Under R.C. 319.202, the buyer files a statement of value and the grantor pays the state-authorized conveyance fee. The statute defines value for a sale as the full consideration, including any mortgage or vendor's lien on the property, and it makes willful falsification of value unlawful. Gifts use estimated market value.

A separate county transfer tax exists in Ohio law: R.C. 322.02 lets a county levy up to 30 cents per $100 by commissioner resolution. The Summit fee page lists a conveyance fee and a lot fee and no other transfer charge. Ask the Property Transfer Department whether anything beyond those two applies to your deed.

One more duty falls on the deed. If the home is residential rental property, the auditor's endorsement notes that the buyer must file rental information under R.C. 5323.02.

sections.h2: Which liens and releases can appear on a Summit County record?
sections.html:
The Recorder Division files encumbrances that bear on title, so a lien search by your title company often turns up items recorded here. The fee page prices several of them, and a release is usually what clears a record before a closing:

  • IRS lien: $5.00. IRS release: $3.00.
  • Workers' compensation lien and its release: no fee.
  • Unemployment lien: no fee. Its release: $4.00.
  • Plats: $0.05 per square inch, with posted sizes running from $40.00 for 11 by 17 inches to $86.40 for 24 by 36 inches.
  • Township zoning regulations: $50.00. Township zoning amendments: $20.00.

Uniform Commercial Code filings carry their own fees, and the page sends callers to 330-643-8143. A mortgage release follows the same path as a deed: the lender or its agent presents it, and the division indexes it so the earlier lien shows as cleared.

Ask your title company for the recording references of anything it finds, since the recording guide asks submitters to cite earlier documents by number, book and page, or recording date.

sections.h2: How do I fix a name, a missing deed or a mistake on a Summit County record?
sections.html:
A recorded deed cannot be edited. The FAQ says a new deed must be prepared and recorded to change a name, and that only the person asking for the change or an attorney may prepare it. The new deed then goes back through the Property Transfer Department for the legal description and transfer before recording.

If you cannot find your own deed, request a copy by mail. Birth and death certificates are not kept here. Summit County Public Health issues them. The Veterans Service Commission helps with a lost DD 214 that was never recorded.

The office also mentions that a tax bill's mailing address changes only by written request from the taxpayer to the Fiscal Officer, which is separate from anything on the deed.

sections.h2: What does Summit County look like to someone selling a house?
sections.html:
QuickFacts shows 538,376 residents for 2025 and 250,438 housing units, with median household income of $71,622. Owners occupy 67.5 percent of homes, and the middle owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 sits at $208,700. Median gross rent is $1,026, and 35.8 percent of adults 25 and older hold at least a bachelor's degree.

Akron is the seat. Wikipedia lists Barberton, Cuyahoga Falls, Fairlawn, Green, Hudson, Macedonia, Munroe Falls, New Franklin, Norton, Stow, Tallmadge and Twinsburg among the cities, and notes that the Fiscal Officer exercises the duties of auditor, treasurer and recorder. In a sale, the legal description check, the conveyance statement and the recording therefore all run through one county office.

faqs.q: How long does Summit County take to record a deed?
faqs.a: The Recorder Division posts a turnaround of 3 to 5 working days. The Property Transfer Department can finish the title transfer the same business day if the forms arrive by 3:30 p.m.

faqs.q: Can a deed be recorded electronically in Summit County?
faqs.a: Yes. The Fiscal Office works with Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners Network, and title companies commonly use them.

faqs.q: Does the Recorder search my title?
faqs.a: No. The division says it performs no title or property searches. Your title company or attorney does that work.

faqs.q: Who must prepare a new deed to change a name?
faqs.a: Only the person requesting the change or an attorney. The new deed is recorded after the Property Transfer Department approves it.

faqs.q: Which Summit County records are not viewable online?
faqs.a: Military discharges. The website shows recorded documents from 1988 forward, and older index books from 1840 to 1988 open in the archive viewer.
